title: Variables & Data Types
description: Learn how JavaScript stores information using variables and understand the different types of values your programs can work with.

sections.title: What Are Variables?
sections.content: A variable is a named container used to store a value in a JavaScript program. Instead of working directly with a value every time, we give it a name and use that name later. Variables are useful when information needs to be stored, reused, displayed, or changed during program execution.

examples.title: Storing a player's name
examples.code:
const playerName = "Shadow";
console.log(playerName);
examples.explanation: The variable playerName stores the string value "Shadow". We can use playerName anywhere we need the player's name.

examples.title: Storing a changing value
examples.explanation: Because health can change during the game, let is appropriate here. The value is changed from 100 to 75.

sections.title: let, const and var
sections.content: JavaScript provides three keywords for declaring variables: let, const, and var. In modern JavaScript, let and const are preferred. Use const when a variable should not be reassigned, and let when its value needs to change. var is an older declaration style that you may still encounter in existing JavaScript code.

examples.title: const
examples.code:
const username = "Alex";
console.log(username);
examples.explanation: Use const when the variable should not be reassigned. const is block-scoped, meaning it is only accessible inside the block where it is declared.

examples.title: let
examples.explanation: Use let when the value needs to be reassigned. let is also block-scoped, meaning it is only accessible inside the block where it is declared.

examples.title: var
examples.explanation: var allows reassignment and is function-scoped rather than block-scoped. It has older scoping behavior, so modern JavaScript generally prefers let and const.

sections.title: Understanding Scope
sections.content:
Scope determines where a variable can be accessed in your code.

### What is a block?

A block is a section of code surrounded by curly braces `{ }`.

...

### Quick comparison

| Declaration | Can be reassigned? | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| `const` | No | Block scope |
| `let` | Yes | Block scope |
| `var` | Yes | Function scope |

Modern JavaScript generally prefers `const` and `let` because their block-scoping behavior makes code easier to understand and reduces accidental access to variables from places where they should not be used.

sections.title: What Are Data Types?
sections.content: A data type describes what kind of value is stored in a variable. JavaScript is dynamically typed, which means a variable does not have to be permanently associated with one data type. Understanding data types is important because different values support different operations.

examples.title: Different types of values
examples.explanation: Here we store three different kinds of values: a string, a number, and a boolean.

sections.title: JavaScript's Main Data Types
sections.content: JavaScript has eight main data types. Seven are primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, and symbol. The eighth is object, which is used for more complex data structures. Arrays and functions are also objects in JavaScript, although they are commonly discussed separately because they are so important.

examples.title: String
examples.code: const playerName = "Shadow";
examples.explanation: Strings represent text. They are commonly used for names, messages, usernames, addresses, and other text-based information.

examples.title: Number
examples.explanation: Numbers represent integer and decimal numeric values. They are used for scores, health, prices, quantities, measurements, and calculations.

examples.title: Boolean
examples.code:
const isOnline = true;
const hasPremium = false;
examples.explanation: Booleans represent either true or false. They are commonly used for conditions, permissions, states, and feature flags.

examples.title: Undefined
examples.code:
let selectedCharacter;
console.log(selectedCharacter);
examples.explanation: A variable that has been declared but has not been assigned a value contains undefined.

examples.title: Null
examples.code: const selectedWeapon = null;
examples.explanation: null is used when we intentionally represent the absence of a value.

examples.title: Object
examples.explanation: Objects group related information together using key-value pairs. They are useful for representing entities such as players, products, users, or orders.

examples.title: Array
examples.code: const inventory = ["Sword", "Shield", "Potion"];
examples.explanation: Arrays store ordered collections of values. They are commonly used for inventories, lists of users, products, scores, and many other collections.

sections.title: The typeof Operator
sections.content: The typeof operator lets us check the type of a value at runtime. This can be useful when debugging, validating data, or understanding what a variable currently contains.

examples.title: Checking data types
examples.explanation: typeof returns "string", "number", and "boolean" for these three values.

examples.title: A common JavaScript surprise
examples.code:
const value = null;
console.log(typeof value);
examples.explanation: JavaScript returns "object" for typeof null. This is a historical behavior in the language and is something developers should know.

sections.title: Real-World Usage
sections.content: Choosing appropriate variable declarations and data types makes programs easier to understand and maintain. Different applications naturally use different types of information.

examples.title: Gaming
examples.explanation: A game might use strings for names, numbers for health and scores, and booleans for player states.

examples.title: E-commerce
examples.explanation: An online store can use strings for product names, numbers for prices and stock, and booleans for availability.

examples.title: Social Media
examples.explanation: A social platform can represent usernames as strings, follower counts as numbers, and verification status as booleans.

mcqTest.explanation: A boolean clearly represents a yes/no state such as product availability.

title: Operators & Conditions
description: Learn how JavaScript calculates values, compares information, combines conditions, and makes decisions using operators and conditional statements.

sections.title: Expressions & Operators
sections.content:
An **expression** is a piece of JavaScript code that produces a value. Operators are symbols or keywords that tell JavaScript how to work with those values.

For example, `5 + 3` is an expression that produces the value `8`. The `+` symbol is an operator.

Operators are fundamental to programming because programs constantly need to calculate values, compare information, and make decisions.

A useful mental model is:

**Values → Operations → New values**

For example:

```js
const price = 100;
const discount = 20;
const finalPrice = price - discount;

console.log(finalPrice);
```

JavaScript takes the values `100` and `20`, applies the subtraction operator, and produces `80`.

As you continue learning JavaScript, you will use operators everywhere: calculating scores, checking permissions, validating forms, processing shopping carts, and controlling game logic.

examples.title: Calculating a game score
examples.explanation: The addition operator combines two numeric values to produce a new value. This same pattern appears in games, finance, shopping carts, and many other applications.

sections.title: Arithmetic Operators
sections.content:
Arithmetic operators are used to perform mathematical calculations.

The most common arithmetic operators are:

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+` | Addition | `10 + 5` |
| `-` | Subtraction | `10 - 5` |
| `*` | Multiplication | `10 * 5` |
| `/` | Division | `10 / 5` |
| `%` | Remainder | `10 % 3` |

The remainder operator `%` is especially useful in programming. It gives you what is left over after division.

```js
console.log(10 % 3);
```

This produces `1` because 3 fits into 10 three times with 1 remaining.

Arithmetic operators are commonly used when working with quantities such as health, points, prices, inventory, distances, and time.

Remember that the `+` operator can also be used with strings. When strings are involved, JavaScript can combine them instead of performing numerical addition.

examples.title: Updating player health
examples.explanation: Arithmetic operators allow a program to update values as something happens. Here, taking damage reduces the player's health by 25.

examples.title: Using the remainder operator
examples.explanation: The remainder operator is useful for determining whether values divide evenly and for patterns such as alternating turns or checking whether a number is even or odd.

sections.title: Assignment & Updating Values

examples.title: Updating a player's score
examples.explanation: The `+=` operator updates the existing value by adding another value. This is common when a game awards points or an application updates a counter.

sections.title: Comparison Operators
sections.content:
Comparison operators are used to ask questions about values. The result of a comparison is always a **boolean**: either `true` or `false`.

Common comparison operators include:

| Operator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `>` | Greater than |
| `<` | Less than |
| `>=` | Greater than or equal to |
| `<=` | Less than or equal to |
| `===` | Strictly equal to |
| `!==` | Strictly not equal to |

For example:

```js
const score = 75;

console.log(score >= 50);
```

JavaScript evaluates the comparison and produces `true`.

This is important because conditions are built from these boolean results. A program can use the result to decide what should happen next.

examples.title: Checking whether a player passed
examples.explanation: The comparison produces a boolean value that can later be used by an `if` statement to decide whether the player passed.

sections.title: Strict Equality: === vs ==
sections.content:
JavaScript provides two common equality operators: `==` and `===`.

The `==` operator performs **loose equality**. It may convert values before comparing them.

The `===` operator performs **strict equality**. It checks both the value and the data type.

For example:

```js
console.log(5 == "5");
console.log(5 === "5");
```

The first comparison can produce `true` because JavaScript converts the values during the comparison. The second produces `false` because one value is a number and the other is a string.

In modern JavaScript development, `===` is generally preferred because it makes comparisons more predictable and avoids unexpected type conversion.

The same principle applies to inequality: prefer `!==` when you need to check that values are strictly different.

examples.title: Avoiding unexpected comparisons
examples.explanation: The first comparison is false because the types are different. The second is true because both the value and type match. Strict equality makes this behavior explicit.

sections.title: Boolean Logic
sections.content:
Comparison operators answer individual questions, but real programs often need to evaluate several conditions together. JavaScript provides logical operators for this.

The three important logical operators are:

| Operator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `&&` | AND |
| `||` | OR |
| `!` | NOT |

`&&` requires both conditions to be true.

```js
age >= 18 && hasTicket
```

`||` requires at least one condition to be true.

```js
isAdmin || isModerator
```

`!` reverses a boolean value.

```js
!isLoggedIn
```

These operators allow you to express more realistic rules instead of checking only one condition at a time.

examples.title: Checking access to a game area
examples.explanation: Both conditions must be true before access is granted. Combining conditions like this is common in authentication and authorization logic.

examples.title: Checking multiple valid roles
examples.explanation: The OR operator allows either condition to satisfy the requirement. This is useful when multiple types of users can perform the same action.

sections.title: Making Decisions with if

examples.title: Checking whether a player has enough health
examples.explanation: The condition determines whether the message should be printed. Decision-making like this is fundamental to game logic and application behavior.

sections.title: else and else if

examples.title: Determining player rank
examples.explanation: Multiple branches allow a program to choose between several outcomes. Notice that the most restrictive condition is checked first.

sections.title: Truthiness & Falsy Values
sections.content:
JavaScript does not always require a condition to be explicitly `true` or `false`. Values can be evaluated in a boolean context.

Values that behave like `false` are called **falsy**. Common falsy values include:

- `false`
- `0`
- `""` (an empty string)
- `null`
- `undefined`
- `NaN`

Most other values behave like `true` and are called **truthy**.

For example:

```js
const username = "Alex";

if (username) {
  console.log("Username exists");
}
```

Because a non-empty string is truthy, the code runs.

Truthiness is useful, but beginners should be careful not to confuse it with strict equality. For example, `0` is falsy, but it is still a valid number. Always think about what the value represents before relying on truthiness.

examples.title: Checking for a username
examples.explanation: An application can use truthiness to determine whether a value has been provided. This pattern appears frequently in form validation and user interfaces.

sections.title: Writing Conditions Clearly

examples.title: Readable permission check
examples.explanation: Parentheses make the intended logic easier to understand. Good developers think about both correctness and readability when writing conditions.

title: Loops & Iteration
description: Learn how to repeat code efficiently using for, while, and do...while loops, and control iterations with break and continue.

sections.title: Why Do We Need Loops?
sections.content: Loops allow you to repeat a block of code without writing the same statements again and again. They are useful when working with repeated tasks, collections of data, and game logic.

examples.title: Repeating a message
examples.explanation: Writing the same statement repeatedly becomes inefficient. A loop allows us to repeat the operation with much less code.

sections.title: The for Loop
sections.content: The for loop is commonly used when you know how many times an operation should repeat. It has three main parts: initialization, condition, and update.

examples.title: Count from 1 to 5
examples.explanation: The loop starts with i equal to 1, continues while i is less than or equal to 5, and increases i by 1 after every iteration.

sections.title: Understanding Initialization, Condition and Update
sections.content: A for loop normally begins by initializing a variable, checks a condition before each iteration, and updates the variable after the loop body executes.

examples.title: Counting by 2
examples.explanation: The loop starts at 0 and increases i by 2 after each iteration, producing even numbers from 0 to 10.

sections.title: The while Loop
sections.content: A while loop repeats as long as its condition remains true. It is useful when the number of iterations is not known in advance.

examples.title: Using while
examples.explanation: The condition is checked before every iteration. The count must be updated or the loop could continue forever.

sections.title: The do...while Loop
sections.content: A do...while loop executes its body at least once because the condition is checked after the loop body.

examples.title: Runs at least once
examples.explanation: Even though number is already 10 and the condition is false, the body executes once before the condition is checked.

sections.title: break
sections.content: The break statement immediately exits the loop. It is useful when you have found what you are looking for or when a condition requires the loop to stop early.

examples.title: Stop when a value is found
examples.explanation: When i reaches 5, break exits the loop immediately, so 5 and the remaining numbers are not printed.

sections.title: continue
sections.content: The continue statement skips the current iteration and moves to the next iteration of the loop.

examples.title: Skip an iteration
examples.explanation: When i is 3, continue skips the rest of that iteration. The loop then continues with 4.

sections.title: Nested Loops
sections.content: A loop can be placed inside another loop. This is called a nested loop and is useful for working with grids, tables, combinations, and other multi-level structures.

examples.title: Nested loop
examples.explanation: For every row, the inner loop runs through all three columns.

sections.title: Avoiding Infinite Loops
sections.content: An infinite loop occurs when a loop condition never becomes false. Always make sure the variables involved in the condition can eventually reach a state that ends the loop.

examples.title: Correctly updating the counter
examples.explanation: The counter increases during every iteration, so eventually count becomes 3 and the condition becomes false.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Loop
sections.content: Use a for loop when the number of iterations is known or controlled by a counter. Use while when repetition depends mainly on a condition. Use do...while when the operation must happen at least once.

examples.title: Game countdown
examples.explanation: A for loop is a natural choice because the countdown has a clear starting value and ending condition.

title: Functions
description: Learn how to create reusable blocks of code using functions, parameters, return values, and arrow functions.

sections.title: What Are Functions?
sections.content: A function is a reusable block of code designed to perform a specific task. Instead of writing the same code repeatedly, you can place it inside a function and call it whenever you need it.

examples.title: A simple function
examples.explanation: The function is declared with the name greet and called using greet().

sections.title: Creating and Calling Functions
sections.content: A function is created using the function keyword followed by a name and parentheses. The code inside the braces runs when the function is called.

examples.title: Calling a function
examples.explanation: Defining a function does not execute it. The function runs when it is called.

sections.title: Parameters and Arguments
sections.content: Parameters allow a function to receive information. The values passed to those parameters when calling the function are called arguments.

examples.title: Using a parameter
examples.explanation: name is the parameter, while "Shadow" is the argument passed to the function.

sections.title: Return Values
sections.content: Functions can return a value using the return statement. The returned value can then be stored in a variable or used in another expression.

examples.title: Returning a value
examples.explanation: The function returns 15, which is stored in result.

sections.title: Multiple Parameters
sections.content: A function can accept multiple parameters. Each argument is matched with the corresponding parameter based on its position.

examples.title: Multiple parameters
examples.explanation: The first argument is assigned to attack and the second argument is assigned to bonus.

sections.title: Function Expressions
sections.content: A function can also be stored inside a variable. This is called a function expression.

examples.title: Function expression
examples.explanation: The function is assigned to the greet variable and called using greet().

sections.title: Arrow Functions
sections.content: Arrow functions provide a shorter syntax for writing functions. They are commonly used in modern JavaScript.

examples.title: Arrow function
examples.explanation: The arrow function syntax makes the function shorter while still accepting parameters and returning a value.

sections.title: Default Parameters
sections.content: Default parameters allow you to provide a fallback value when an argument is not supplied.

examples.title: Default parameter
examples.explanation: If no name is provided, JavaScript uses the default value "Player".

sections.title: Function Scope
sections.content: Variables declared inside a function are generally available only inside that function. This helps keep data organized and prevents unrelated code from changing it.

examples.title: Local variable
examples.explanation: The score variable belongs to the function and is available inside its scope.

sections.title: Writing Reusable Functions
sections.content: Good functions usually perform one clear task and can be reused with different values. Breaking a program into small functions makes code easier to understand and maintain.

examples.title: Reusable game function
examples.explanation: The same function can calculate the remaining health for different players or situations.

title: Arrays
description: Learn how to store collections of values, access individual elements, modify arrays, and iterate through their contents.

sections.title: What Are Arrays?
Creating Arrays
sections.content:
Arrays are created using square brackets `[]`. The values inside the brackets are separated by commas.

```js
const players = ["Alex", "Sam", "John"];
```

An array can contain different types of values, although it is usually easier to work with arrays containing related types of data.

```js
const scores = [100, 250, 500];
const onlinePlayers = [true, false, true];
```

You can also create an empty array and add values later:

```js
const inventory = [];
```

Arrays can grow or shrink during program execution, even when declared with `const`.

sections.title: Array Indexing
sections.content:
Array indexes start at **0**, not 1. The first element has index `0`, the second has index `1`, and so on.

```js
const weapons = ["Sword", "Bow", "Axe"];

console.log(weapons[0]);
console.log(weapons[1]);
console.log(weapons[2]);
```

The output is:

```text
Sword
Bow
Axe
```

Remember: **index = position - 1** when thinking about human counting.

sections.title: Changing Array Elements
Adding Elements with push
sections.content:
The `push()` method adds one or more elements to the end of an array.

```js
const inventory = ["Sword", "Shield"];

inventory.push("Potion");

console.log(inventory);
```

The resulting array is:

```text
["Sword", "Shield", "Potion"]
```

`push()` is useful when new items need to be added to a collection.

sections.title: Removing Elements with pop
The length Property
sections.content:
The `length` property tells you how many elements are currently stored in an array.

```js
const players = ["Alex", "Sam", "John"];

console.log(players.length);
```

This prints `3`.

The last element can be accessed using `length - 1`:

```js
console.log(players[players.length - 1]);
```

title: Array Methods
description: Learn how to process and transform arrays using powerful methods such as forEach, map, filter, find, and reduce.

sections.title: Why Array Methods?
sections.content:
Loops allow you to process arrays, but JavaScript also provides built-in array methods that make common operations easier to express.

For example, instead of manually creating a new array while looping through numbers, you can use `map()`.

Array methods are widely used in modern JavaScript, especially when working with API data, React applications, and collections of objects.

sections.title: forEach
map
filter
find
reduce
Method Chaining
sections.content:
Array methods can be combined together. This is called **method chaining**.

For example, you can filter values and then transform the remaining values:

```js
const scores = [40, 60, 80, 90];

const result = scores
  .filter((score) => score >= 50)
  .map((score) => score * 2);

console.log(result);
```

First, `filter()` keeps the passing scores. Then `map()` doubles those scores.

Method chaining can make data-processing logic concise, but each step should remain understandable.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Method
sections.content:
Different array methods solve different problems.

| Method | Main purpose | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `forEach()` | Perform an action for each element | `undefined` |
| `map()` | Transform every element | New array |
| `filter()` | Select matching elements | New array |
| `find()` | Find the first matching element | Element or `undefined` |
| `reduce()` | Combine elements into one result | Single value |

A useful way to remember them is:

- **forEach** → Do something
- **map** → Transform
- **filter** → Select
- **find** → Find one
- **reduce** → Combine

title: DOM & Events
description: Learn how JavaScript interacts with web pages by selecting elements, changing content and styles, and responding to user actions.

sections.title: What Is the DOM?
sections.content:
The **DOM (Document Object Model)** is a representation of an HTML page that JavaScript can interact with. The browser creates a tree-like structure from the HTML document, allowing JavaScript to read and modify elements.

For example, an HTML element such as a button becomes an object that JavaScript can access and manipulate.

sections.title: Selecting Elements
sections.content:
JavaScript provides several methods for finding elements on a page. Common methods include `getElementById()` and `querySelector()`.

`querySelector()` is especially useful because it can select elements using CSS selectors.

examples.title: Selecting an element
examples.code:
const title = document.querySelector("h1");
const button = document.querySelector("button");
examples.explanation: Once an element is selected, JavaScript can read or modify it.

sections.title: Changing Text Content
sections.content: The `textContent` property allows JavaScript to change the text inside an element.

examples.title: Changing text
examples.code:
const title = document.querySelector("h1");
title.textContent = "Welcome to Mentor AI";
examples.explanation: The heading changes immediately when JavaScript updates its textContent.

sections.title: Changing Styles
sections.content: JavaScript can also modify an element's style through the `style` property.

examples.title: Changing a style
examples.code:
const title = document.querySelector("h1");
title.style.fontSize = "32px";
examples.explanation: JavaScript can dynamically change how an element appears.

sections.title: What Are Events?
sections.content:
An **event** represents something that happens in the browser. Examples include clicking a button, typing into an input, moving the mouse, or submitting a form.

JavaScript can listen for these events and respond to them.

sections.title: addEventListener
sections.content: The `addEventListener()` method allows JavaScript to listen for an event and execute a function when that event occurs.

examples.title: Listening for a click
examples.explanation: The function runs whenever the user clicks the button.

sections.title: Event Objects
sections.content: When an event occurs, JavaScript can provide information about that event through an event object.

examples.title: Using the event object
examples.explanation: The target property identifies the element that triggered the event.

sections.title: Handling Input
sections.content: Events are commonly used with form controls such as input fields. JavaScript can read the current value and respond when the user interacts with the field.

examples.title: Reading an input
examples.explanation: The input event runs whenever the user changes the field.

sections.title: Preventing Default Behavior
sections.content: Some browser events have default behavior. For example, submitting a form normally causes the browser to submit the form. `preventDefault()` can stop that behavior when JavaScript needs to handle the action itself.

examples.title: Preventing form submission
examples.explanation: This allows JavaScript to control what happens when the form is submitted.

sections.title: DOM in Real Applications
sections.content: The DOM is the foundation of interactive web interfaces. JavaScript uses it to update content, respond to users, display messages, validate forms, control menus, and create dynamic experiences.

title: Asynchronous JavaScript
description: Learn how JavaScript handles tasks that take time using callbacks, promises, async functions, await, and API requests.

sections.title: What Is Asynchronous JavaScript?
sections.content:
JavaScript often needs to perform tasks that do not finish immediately, such as requesting data from a server or waiting for a timer.

Asynchronous JavaScript allows the program to continue running while waiting for these tasks to complete.

sections.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous
sections.content: Synchronous code runs one operation after another. Asynchronous operations can begin a task and allow other code to continue before the task finishes.

sections.title: setTimeout
sections.content: `setTimeout()` schedules a function to run after a specified amount of time.

examples.title: Delayed execution
examples.explanation: The delayed function runs later while the rest of the program continues.

sections.title: Callbacks
sections.content: A callback is a function passed to another function so it can be executed later. Callbacks are commonly used with asynchronous operations.

sections.title: Promises
sections.content: A Promise represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. A promise can be pending, fulfilled, or rejected.

examples.title: Creating a Promise
examples.explanation: then() runs when the promise is successfully fulfilled.

sections.title: then and catch
sections.content: `then()` handles a successful promise result, while `catch()` handles a rejected promise.

examples.title: Handling a promise
examples.explanation: This separates successful results from errors.

sections.title: async Functions
sections.content: An `async` function always returns a Promise. It allows asynchronous code to be written in a style that looks more like normal synchronous code.

sections.title: await
sections.content: The `await` keyword pauses execution inside an async function until a Promise settles.

examples.title: Using await
examples.explanation: await makes it easier to work with the result of an asynchronous operation.

sections.title: Fetching Data from APIs
sections.content: The `fetch()` function is commonly used to request data from web APIs. It returns a Promise containing the response.

examples.title: Fetching API data
examples.explanation: The response can be converted to JSON and then used by the application.

sections.title: Async JavaScript in Real Applications
sections.content: Asynchronous JavaScript is essential for modern web applications. It is used when communicating with APIs, loading data, authenticating users, uploading files, and communicating with backend services.

title: Error Handling & Debugging
description: Learn how to understand JavaScript errors, handle failures safely, and debug programs using practical techniques.

sections.title: What Are Errors?
sections.content:
Errors occur when JavaScript cannot successfully execute code. Errors can happen because of invalid syntax, incorrect values, missing variables, or problems during program execution.

Learning to understand errors is an essential part of programming.

sections.title: Syntax Errors
sections.content: A syntax error occurs when JavaScript code does not follow the language's syntax rules.

examples.title: Syntax error
examples.code:
const name = "Shadow";
console.log(name
examples.explanation: The closing parenthesis is missing, so JavaScript cannot correctly parse the code.

sections.title: Runtime Errors
sections.content: A runtime error occurs while the program is executing. The code may be syntactically valid but still attempt an invalid operation.

examples.title: Runtime error
examples.code:
const player = null;
console.log(player.name);
examples.explanation: The program attempts to access a property from null, which causes a runtime error.

sections.title: Reference Errors
sections.content: A ReferenceError commonly occurs when code tries to use a variable that does not exist in the current scope.

examples.title: ReferenceError
examples.code: console.log(playerName);
examples.explanation: If playerName has not been declared, JavaScript cannot find the referenced variable.

sections.title: Type Errors
sections.content: A TypeError occurs when an operation is performed on a value that does not support that operation.

examples.title: TypeError
examples.code:
const score = 100;
score.toUpperCase();
examples.explanation: Numbers do not have the toUpperCase() method, so JavaScript throws a TypeError.

sections.title: try and catch
sections.content: The `try...catch` statement allows JavaScript to handle errors without immediately stopping the surrounding program.

examples.title: Handling an error
examples.explanation: If an error occurs inside try, execution moves to the catch block.

sections.title: The Error Object
sections.content: The value received by `catch` often contains information about the error. Common properties include `name` and `message`.

examples.title: Reading an error
examples.explanation: The message property describes why the error occurred.

sections.title: throw
sections.content: The `throw` statement allows a program to create and raise an error intentionally.

examples.title: Throwing an error
examples.explanation: throw allows a function to signal that an invalid situation has occurred.

sections.title: Debugging Techniques
sections.content: Debugging means finding and fixing problems in a program. Useful techniques include reading error messages, using `console.log()`, checking variable values, and using browser developer tools.

sections.title: Debugging in Real Applications
sections.content: Professional developers constantly debug applications. Understanding error messages and isolating problems makes it easier to fix bugs quickly and build reliable software.
